lineage_context.teaching_goal: Use Pilostyles as an extreme evolutionary contrast: a chlorophyll-free endoparasite in Cucurbitales whose vegetative body is hidden inside a host and whose flowers erupt through the host stem.

project_scope.note: The current project contains Pilostyles thurberi, accepted by Kew and native from the southwestern/south-central U.S. into Mexico, including Texas.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: examine legume host stems for tiny flower structures breaking through bark; verify overlapping perianth parts and the reproductive center rather than identifying any reddish bump as Pilostyles.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Achlorophyllous endoparasite. No normal exposed roots, stems or leaves; the vegetative body consists of filamentous tissue embedded within host stems, superficially reminiscent of fungal hyphae.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Pilostyles thurberi has tiny unisexual flowers with overlapping tepal-like parts. Staminate flowers bear central pollen sacs in a synandrium; pistillate flowers have stigmatic papillae above a semi-inferior ovary. Both sexes may appear on one host, which does not establish that they belong to one parasite individual.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Small fleshy berry-like fruit developing at the host-stem surface, containing numerous tiny seeds.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Tiny red-brown flowers apparently growing straight out of a Dalea or other legume stem, with no visible parasite leaves or shoots, is the Pilostyles/Apodanthaceae doorway.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: host plant → bark eruption → tiny scale-ringed flower → hidden endophyte concept → fruit → Cucurbitaceae evolutionary contrast
visual_lesson.intro: Apodanthaceae may be the strangest family in the learner: almost the entire plant is hidden inside another plant.

steps.title: 1 · Find the host before the parasite
steps.look_for: A normal-looking legume stem carrying tiny reddish-brown bumps/flowers directly on the stem surface.
steps.why_it_matters: There is no ordinary exposed parasite shoot to search for.

steps.title: 2 · Zoom into the flower erupting through bark
steps.look_for: Tiny flowers emerging through host cortical tissue, surrounded by several whorls of fleshy scale-like bracts/perianth structures.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the visible organism most of the year when reproductive.

steps.title: 3 · Learn the invisible vegetative body
steps.look_for: Threadlike parasite tissue embedded internally in the host rather than a separate leafy stem.
steps.why_it_matters: Explains why Apodanthaceae looks nothing like its Cucurbitales relatives.

steps.title: 4 · Separate male and female flowers
steps.look_for: Pilostyles has unisexual flowers; staminate flowers bear sessile anthers around the central column, while pistillate flowers carry the receptive structures.
steps.why_it_matters: Connects the radically reduced flower back to ordinary angiosperm reproductive roles.

steps.title: 5 · Follow it into the small fruit
steps.look_for: Small fleshy fruits remain attached directly to the host surface and contain numerous tiny seeds.

comparisons.title: Apodanthaceae vs Cucurbitaceae
comparisons.rule: They share Cucurbitales ancestry but almost no field gestalt: Cucurbitaceae is green, leafy and usually tendril-bearing; Apodanthaceae is an achlorophyllous endoparasite whose flowers emerge directly from host stems.

comparisons.title: Pilostyles vs mistletoes/Santalaceae
comparisons.rule: Mistletoes expose their own green or leafy shoots outside the host. Pilostyles keeps nearly all vegetative tissue inside the host and exposes mainly flowers/fruits.

comparisons.title: Pilostyles vs fungi/galls
comparisons.rule: The internal body may resemble fungal strands and the flowers can look gall-like, but the exposed structures are true angiosperm flowers and fruits with reproductive organs/seeds.

comparisons.title: Pilostyles versus host buds, fruits, galls and fungi
comparisons.rule: Host buds or pods belong to the legume; galls or fungi can produce bumps but do not contain confirmed Pilostyles floral organs. Verify the true bark-emerging flower with overlapping tepals and a reproductive center. Color alone is insufficient.

visual_lesson.caveat: Host association is important but not sufficient: Pilostyles thurberi parasitizes legumes, especially Dalea and relatives. Confirm the distinctive stem-erupting flowers rather than assuming every bump on a host stem is the parasite.

anatomy_examples.look_for: Matched entire legume stem and macro of actual flower at bark showing perianth, separately identifying parasite and host.
anatomy_examples.photo_role: exact-taxon host branch and flower emergence macro
anatomy_examples.caption: A flower emerges through the host stem, not from an independent green parasite shoot.

anatomy_examples.botanical_label: staminate synandrium and pistillate stigmatic papillae
anatomy_examples.look_for: Verified staminate and pistillate close-ups in comparable views; reproductive structures actually visible.
anatomy_examples.caption: Determine flower sex from visible reproductive structures, never from the host branch.

anatomy_examples.plain_label: Surface fruit and hidden parasite threads
anatomy_examples.botanical_label: mature fruit with seeds and endophytic filaments
anatomy_examples.look_for: Verified berry developing from a flower on host bark and a separately sourced anatomical host-stem section of embedded parasitic tissue.
anatomy_examples.photo_role: exact-taxon fruit macro with separately labeled tissue-section reference
anatomy_examples.caption: The fruit is visible outside the host; most vegetative tissue remains embedded within it.

genera.fast_cue: leafless endoparasite inside legume stems; only tiny flowers/fruits visibly erupt through host bark

visual_targets.structure: Pilostyles flowers erupting from host stem
visual_targets.annotation_goal: label host bark and parasite flower separately
show hidden filamentous vegetative tissue inside host
show extreme morphological divergence within Cucurbitales
